newsitem.title: UK: International pressure mounts against IRA attacks.
newsitem.headline: International pressure mounts against IRA attacks.

text.p: The IRA came under fierce international pressure to end its murderous campaign in Northern Ireland on Tuesday after a guerrilla ambush killed two police officers and shrouded peace attempts in gloom.

The province's police chief said there was no sign of the IRA ending hostilities and his officers were on alert in case of British Prime Minister Tony Blair renewed a charge that Irish Republican Army guerrillas who ambushed the officers in the town of Lurgan on Monday had set out to sabotage an Anglo-Irish peace initiative.
U.S. President Bill Clinton castigated the IRA for "this brutal act of terrorism".
"There is nothing patriotic or heroic about these cowardly killings," said Clinton in a written statement issued on Monday night. He also warned against retaliation by pro-British Loyalists.
European Union leaders meeting in Amsterdam said they were horrified at the double murder. They reaffirmed "abhorrence of terrorist violence in all its forms".

Blair, whose condemnation has been backed by outgoing Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, accused Irish republicans of bad faith over a peace process that has been dogged by violence since the end of an IRA ceasefire in February 1996.

Britain broke off tentative contacts with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, immediately after the ambush. London and Dublin have insisted that the IRA call a ceasefire before they will invite Sinn Fein to talks.
Blair said in Amsterdam that the EU had taken the unusual step of issuing a unanimous statement about the atrocity because the guerrillas had made a "deliberate attempt to stop" the peace process.

"So it's not merely our repugnance at the killing and our deep sympathy for the families, it's that there is such a serious element of bad faith ...and I think the Americans, as everyone else has been, have been really shocked by this."

Faced with further isolation, Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, said his party would continue to try and bring about "real and meaningful and inclusive peace negotiations" but agreed the killings had created a "very dangerous situation".
He declined to condemn the shootings during a BBC radio interview, but described them as a human tragedy.
Northern Ireland police chief Ronnie Flanagan, who visited the policemen's families on Monday, said he was pessimistic about the immediate future.
"All the indications we have lead us to believe that in the immediate future there is no prospect of a restoration of a cessation of violence," Flanagan warned.
Anxiety grew that there could be a backlash against Catholic nationalists by banned Protestant Loyalist groups.
There was no word from the underground Combined Loyalist Military Command, the umbrella group for outlawed militias loyal to London, whose October 1994 truce has been breached several times recently.
Gary McMichael, leader of the Ulster Democratic Party, the political arm of a banned Protestant guerrilla group, told Sky News that the way forward was through dialogue.
"This is the most critical point we have experienced in recent years and the IRA must recognise the implications of a continued conflict, and they must call an immediate ceasefire."

Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, held further talks with Protestant and Catholic groups whose disputes about contentious July street parades threaten to spill over into serious violence.

Politicians said that the IRA attack was designed to inflame sectarian tension during the traditionally turbulent "marching season" by Protestant Orangemen who loudly trumpet their allegiance to London.
More than 3,200 civilians, police, soldiers and guerrillas have been killed since 1969 in sectarian conflict between majority Protestants and minority Catholics in Northern Ireland.
